title: Antarctic ice holds bubbles of air 800,000 years old
body: As snow piles up on Antarctica, it is squeezed into ice that traps tiny pockets of air. Cores drilled more than 3 km deep give a continuous record of the atmosphere going back about 800,000 years. Over that span, carbon dioxide swung between roughly 180 and 300 parts per million as ice ages came and went. Today it is above 420 ppm, higher than at any point in that record, because of human activity.

slides.heading: Read like tree rings
slides.text: Where snowfall is heavy, yearly layers can be counted like tree rings. Deeper down they thin out, so scientists also date ice by other methods.

slides.heading: The air is younger
slides.text: Snow stays porous for tens of metres before sealing, so the air trapped in a bubble can be centuries to thousands of years younger than the ice around it.

slides.heading: Even older ice
slides.text: In 2016, cores from Antarctica’s Allan Hills, where old ice lies near the surface, held ice dated to about 2.7 million years ago.

slides.question: Why is the air in an ice bubble younger than the ice around it?
options: Snow stays porous before it seals shut
Air leaks in through cracks in the ice
Bubbles slowly rise through the ice
Ice forms faster than snow falls
slides.explanation: Snow stays porous for tens of metres before sealing, so the air trapped in a bubble can be centuries to thousands of years younger than the ice around it.
